room/want: A token's residual stream is a list of d numbers. But a model has far more than d things to track: is the text French, is it inside a quote, does it name a person.
room/feature: Each such property is called a feature, and its value says how strongly it is present. The model stores it along a direction of its own: an arrow.
room/perp: With d of two, two features fit perfectly: one arrow along each axis, at a right angle. Stacked as rows, the arrows make W.
room/store: Give them values, f: three and two. As with an embedding table, f times W adds up each row times its value, so the stream, x, is three, two.
room/read: Dot x with feature zero's arrow, one, zero, and you read back three: exactly its value. The other arrow, at a right angle, adds nothing.
room/limit: But a plane has no third direction at a right angle to both: a stream of width d holds at most d arrows all at right angles.
three/three: To fit a third feature, give up exact right angles: spread three arrows evenly around the circle, a hundred and twenty degrees apart.
three/unit: Each is one unit long, with its tip on the circle of radius one. Feature zero's arrow is still one, zero.
three/self: Dot an arrow with itself, and you get one: one times one, plus zero times zero.
three/pair: Two different arrows give minus a half: one times minus a half, plus zero. Every pair is a hundred and twenty degrees apart, so every pair overlaps by that same minus a half.
read/store: Now store three values: f is three, zero and two. Features zero and two are on, and feature one is off.
read/scale: f times W is three of feature zero's arrow, which is three, zero, plus two of feature two's, which is minus one, minus one point seven four.
read/sum: So the stream, x, is two, and minus one point seven four: three values laid on top of one another in two numbers. That is superposition: placing one thing on top of another.
read/read: Read feature zero back as before: x dot its arrow, one, zero, picks out the first entry of x. Two, not three.
read/split: Why two? x is three of feature zero's arrow plus two of feature two's, so the reading splits: three times one, plus two times minus a half.
read/rule: So a reading is the feature's own value, minus half of each other value that is on. The minus one leaked in from feature two: that leak is called interference.
sparse/sparse: Interference only comes from features that are on together. But most features are sparse, on for few tokens: if each is on for one token in a hundred, two given ones are on together for about one in ten thousand.
sparse/alone: So mostly a feature is on alone. Say only feature two is on, at two: reading feature zero gives minus a half times two, minus one, though it is off.
sparse/relu: A ReLU after the reading keeps positive numbers and zeros the rest: minus one becomes zero, off, as it should be.
sparse/many: And the more dimensions, the gentler the squeeze: only d arrows fit at exact right angles, but far more fit nearly so, overlapping only a little.
sparse/toy: In 2022, in Toy Models of Superposition, Nelson Elhage, Chris Olah and colleagues trained tiny models to squeeze five features into two numbers, with a ReLU after.
sparse/found: With dense features, on most of the time, the models kept only the two most important, at a right angle. With sparse ones, they kept more by letting arrows overlap: five equally important features spread out as a pentagon.
